title: Formation of the Solar System
intro: Where did the Sun, Earth and the other planets come from? Follow the nebular theory step by step: a cloud enriched by earlier stars collapses under gravity, heats up, spins faster and flattens into a disk; metal, rock and, beyond the frost line, ice condense into tiny seeds; the seeds grow by accretion into small rocky planets near the Sun and giant gas-wrapped planets farther out; the solar wind clears the leftover gas; and the leftovers become asteroids and comets that bombard the planets. Then see how captures and giant impacts, including the one that made our Moon, explain the exceptions.

learningObjectives.text: Name the four major features of the solar system that any theory of its formation must explain.
Explain why the close encounter hypothesis was rejected and why the many planetary systems around other stars support the nebular theory.
Describe galactic recycling, give the solar nebula's make-up by mass (98% hydrogen and helium, 2% everything else) and explain why the first stars could not have had planets.
Explain why a collapsing cloud heats up (conservation of energy), spins faster (conservation of angular momentum) and flattens into a disk (collisions).
Use the spinning disk to explain why the planets orbit in the same direction, in nearly the same plane, on nearly circular orbits.
List the four ingredients of the solar nebula from most to least abundant and say which ones condense at which temperatures.
Explain what the frost line is, where it was, and how moving it (for example with a hotter or cooler young Sun) would change where planets form.
Describe how grains grew into planetesimals and planets by accretion, and contrast how the terrestrial and jovian planets and their moons formed.
Explain how the solar wind cleared the nebula, why the Sun spins slowly today, and what would change if the gas had stayed longer or left earlier.
Explain asteroids and comets as leftovers, the heavy bombardment, how Earth got its water, and how giant impacts and captures explain exceptions such as our Moon.

sections.title: What a formation theory must explain

steps.title: Four features to explain
bullets: A theory of how the solar system formed is tested against the **four major features** we see today.
**1. Orderly motions**: every planet circles the Sun the same way, on a nearly circular orbit in almost the same plane, and most of them also spin in that direction.
**2. Two kinds of planets**: close to the Sun, small rocky **terrestrial** planets; farther out, big hydrogen-rich **jovian** planets.
**3. Huge numbers of small bodies**: **asteroids** and **comets**.
**4. A few exceptions**: Venus and Uranus spin backward, Uranus is tipped on its side, and Earth has an unusually large Moon.
A theory that fails even one of these four tests cannot be correct.

steps.title: The close encounter hypothesis
bullets: In the first half of the 1900s, a rival idea said the planets were blobs of gas **pulled out of the Sun** by the gravity of another star that passed very close.
Calculations showed it could not give the planets their **observed orbital motions** and could not explain the neat split into **two types of planets**.
Gas torn from the Sun would share the Sun's make-up, almost all hydrogen and helium, so it gives no reason for small planets of **rock and metal** near the Sun.
It also needed a near-collision between two stars, which is **extremely rare** because stars are so far apart. Planets would then be rare too.
We now know planets orbit a great many stars, so this idea has been **discarded**.

img.alt: An artist's view of a newborn star glowing through a thick, dark ring of dust and gas that surrounds it.

steps.title: The nebular theory
bullets: According to the **nebular theory**, the solar system began when a giant interstellar cloud of gas and dust, the **solar nebula**, underwent **gravitational collapse**.
**Kant** (around 1755) and later **Laplace** proposed the idea more than two centuries ago. **Nebula** is Latin for cloud.
With better physics it explained all four features, so it rose from a hypothesis to a scientific **theory**.
Its biggest test: it says planets are a normal by-product of star birth, so **planetary systems should be common**. Observations of many other planetary systems have confirmed this.

boxes.text: Why test a theory against four features? A theory of origins has to account for what the solar system looks like now. Explaining one feature is easy; explaining all four with the same physics is what makes the nebular theory convincing.
Close encounter = a rare accident, debris torn from the Sun. Nebular = a normal event, a collapsing cloud. Many planetary systems seen around other stars favour the normal event.

The close encounter hypothesis is rejected for three reasons: the wrong orbital motions, no reason for two planet types, and it makes planets rare. Observations of stars forming in disks support the nebular theory; they are not evidence about close encounters themselves. Ch8.1 slide 4 calls it the nebular theory; the hypothesis of Kant and Laplace is its older form.

sections.title: Where the gas came from: galactic recycling

img.alt: A loop of three pictures joined by arrows: stars are born in clouds of gas and dust, stars make heavier elements from lighter ones, and stars return material to space when they die.

steps.title: Stars recycle the galaxy's gas
bullets: The **Big Bang** made almost only **hydrogen and helium**.
Clouds of gas and dust are where stars are born. Inside stars, **nuclear fusion** turns lighter elements into **heavier elements**.
When a star dies it returns its material to space, gently as a **planetary nebula** or violently in a **supernova**. Supernovae also make many other elements.
That enriched gas mixes into interstellar clouds that form the next generation of stars. This loop is **galactic recycling**.

steps.title: What the solar nebula was made of
bullets: Even after billions of years of this recycling, most matter was still the original hydrogen and helium; only a small share had been turned into heavier elements.
By mass the solar nebula was about **98% hydrogen and helium** and only about **2% everything else** combined.
The Sun and the jovian planets are mostly that hydrogen and helium. Earth and the other terrestrial worlds are built almost entirely from the small **2%**.
We are **star stuff**: the atoms in our planet and our bodies were made in stars that lived and died before the Sun formed.

steps.title: The first stars could not have had planets like ours
bullets: The very **first generation** of stars formed from gas that held **only hydrogen and helium**.
Hydrogen and helium never condense into solid grains in a nebula, so there was **no rock, metal or ice** to make solid seeds.
With no solid seeds there could be **no planetesimals**, so no terrestrial planets, no jovian cores, and no asteroids or comets.
Evidence for recycling: **old stars** contain a smaller share of heavy elements than **young stars**, because they formed before much enrichment had happened.

img.alt: Two pictures: a small glowing disk around a young star inside the Orion Nebula, and an infrared image of the dusty disk around the star Beta Pictoris, seen edge-on, with a probable jovian planet marked close to the star.

steps.title: We can watch star systems forming today
bullets: Telescopes show stars being born inside gas clouds like the **Orion Nebula**, many with **disks** of gas and dust around them, the places where planets can form.
An infrared image of the young star **Beta Pictoris** shows a dusty disk seen edge-on and a probable jovian planet orbiting inside it.
Collapsing clouds should heat up and glow in **infrared**, and they do. Some young disks fire **jets** of gas out of their poles.
**Computer simulations** that start from real cloud conditions and apply the laws of physics reproduce the general motions of our solar system.

boxes.text: Why does recycling matter for planets? Only the heavy elements, about 2% of the nebula by mass, can become solid. Without earlier generations of stars there would have been nothing solid to build Earth from.
98 : 2. Ninety-eight percent hydrogen and helium gas that never condenses; two percent everything else, from which every rocky world was made.

Radioactive decay is not a step in galactic recycling and does not refill the galaxy with hydrogen and helium. The steps are: stars form in clouds, fusion makes heavier elements, dying stars return them, new stars form. Ch8.1 slide 5 says elements are released 'in the form of a planetary nebula, or in a supernova explosion'.

sections.title: Collapse: gravity takes over and the cloud heats up

img.alt: A large, ragged cloud with arrows pointing inward shrinks into a smaller, hotter, swirling cloud that is starting to rotate faster.

steps.title: What started and drove the collapse
bullets: The solar nebula began as a huge, cold, thin, roughly round cloud, perhaps a few **light-years** across, turning imperceptibly slowly.
Spread out that much, its own gravity may have been too weak to start a collapse. An outside event, probably the **shock wave of a nearby supernova**, likely gave it a push.
Once started, **gravity** kept it going. The mass stayed the same while the cloud shrank, so gravity grew stronger (an **inverse square law**) and the collapse sped up.
Gravity pulls equally in every direction, which is why the Sun and planets are round. Other laws, not gravity, decided the shape of the nebula itself.

img.alt: An artist's view of a bright young Sun at the centre of a wide, glowing disk of gas and dust.

steps.title: Heating: energy is conserved
bullets: As the cloud shrank, its **gravitational potential energy** turned into **kinetic energy** of gas falling inward.
The falling particles crashed into each other, turning that kinetic energy into random motion, which is **thermal energy**. So the cloud **heated up**. Some energy escaped as light.
This is **conservation of energy** at work: the energy did not appear from nowhere; it changed form.
The centre became the densest and hottest place. There the pressure and temperature finally became high enough to make the **young Sun**.

boxes.text: Why does a shrinking cloud get hot? Gas falling inward speeds up as it loses gravitational potential energy, and collisions convert that speed into heat. No fuel is burned; it is energy changing form.
Shrink = heat (energy) and spin (angular momentum). Gravity starts the collapse squeezing; the conservation laws decide what happens next.

Gravity, not outside pressure, light pressure or electric charge, is what collapses the cloud. A supernova shock wave may trigger the collapse, but gravity does the work. Ch8.2 pt1 slide 3 says the energy became 'heat and light as particles collided'.

sections.title: Spinning faster and flattening into a disk

steps.title: Spinning: angular momentum is conserved
bullets: The cloud spun **faster and faster as it shrank**, the same way an **ice skater pulling in her arms** speeds up. This is **conservation of angular momentum**.
Even a cloud that turned imperceptibly slowly before collapse ends up spinning fast once it is much smaller.
The fast spin stopped everything from falling into the centre. Material orbiting in a disk could stay out of the Sun. The more angular momentum a cloud has, the more **spread out** it ends up.

img.alt: A rotating cloud is squashed into a flat disk by collisions between particles, ending as a spinning, flattened disk with its mass and highest temperature at the centre.

steps.title: Flattening: collisions average out the motions
bullets: Clumps of gas inside the cloud first moved in **random directions** at random speeds.
As the cloud shrank, clumps **collided and merged**, and each merged clump took the **average** motion of the clumps that made it.
Motions up and down cancelled out, but the overall spin did not, so the lumpy cloud settled into a **rotating, flattened disk** with mass and heat concentrated in the centre.
Collisions also made stretched (elliptical) orbits **more circular**. Stir pepper into water at random and it soon settles into one slow swirl, the average of all the stirring.

steps.title: Why the planets move in such an orderly way
bullets: The planets formed **inside the flat disk**, so they orbit in **nearly the same plane**.
The **Sun's rotation** and **every planet's orbit** both go the same way the disk spun.
Computer models show forming planets also tended to **rotate** in that same direction, which is why most planets do. Planets are small compared with the disk, so a few exceptions could arise.

The circularizing effect of collisions explains why planetary orbits are **nearly circular**. Flattened disks appear wherever orbiting particles collide: spiral galaxies, planetary rings and disks around young stars.

img.alt: A wide, glowing disk of gas and dust circles a young star, all of it turning the same way in one flat plane.

boxes.text: Why does a cloud become a disk rather than a smaller ball? Collisions cancel motions that do not match the overall spin, but angular momentum cannot be cancelled. The only arrangement left is material circling in one plane in one direction.
Three outcomes of collapse: HEATS (energy), SPINS faster (angular momentum), FLATTENS (collisions). Heating + spinning + flattening = the orderly solar system.

The disk was not a lucky original shape, and the Sun did not form first and then spread out like spinning pizza dough. Any rotating, collapsing cloud ends up as a spinning disk. A system with planets orbiting in completely different planes would not fit the nebular theory, while a few backward-spinning planets or backward-orbiting small moons would.

sections.title: Ingredients of the nebula and condensation

steps.title: Four kinds of ingredients
bullets: **Hydrogen and helium gas** (about **98%** of the mass) never condense in the nebula.
**Hydrogen compounds** (about **1.4%**): water, methane and ammonia. They freeze into **ices** only below about **150 K**.
**Rock** (about **0.4%**): various minerals, solid below about **500 to 1300 K**.
**Metal** (about **0.2%**): iron, nickel and aluminum, solid below about **1000 to 1600 K**.
From most to least by mass: **hydrogen and helium, hydrogen compounds, rock, metal**. Metal condenses at the **highest** temperature even though it is the scarcest.

img.alt: A top view of the young solar system with a hot grey centre, a rock and metal condensation line, a frost line, and a close-up showing scattered tiny solid grains.

steps.title: Condensation makes the seeds of planets
bullets: In the disk the gas was far too spread out for gravity alone to pull it into planets. Planets needed solid **seeds** first.
**Condensation** is when solid (or liquid) particles form out of a gas, like snowflakes forming in a cold cloud. Pressure in the nebula was too low for liquid droplets, so the particles were solid.
What condensed at each place depended on **temperature**, which fell with distance from the hot centre.
Mixing kept the composition the **same everywhere**; only the temperature changed, and that alone decided which ingredients became solid.

boxes.text: Why did temperature decide what became solid? Each ingredient has its own condensation temperature. Where the nebula was hotter than that temperature, the ingredient stayed gas; where it was cooler, tiny solid grains formed.
Order of abundance: H/He >> hydrogen compounds > rock > metal (98, 1.4, 0.4, 0.2). Order of condensing as it cools: metal first, then rock, then ices; hydrogen and helium never.

Rock is more abundant than metal (0.4% versus 0.2%), and hydrogen compounds outweigh rock and metal together. A list that puts metal above rock, or hydrogen compounds above hydrogen and helium, is wrong. The temperatures are from Table 8.1 of Cosmic Perspective; the Ch8.2 pt1 slides give only the zones.

sections.title: The frost line: two kinds of seeds

img.alt: A glowing disk around the young Sun with a white ring marking the frost line, a hot thermometer inside the ring and a cold thermometer beyond it.

steps.title: Temperature zones in the nebula
bullets: **Right next to the young Sun**: too hot for anything to condense. Rock, metal and hydrogen compounds all stayed gas.
**Near Mercury's orbit**: cool enough for **metals and some rock** to form tiny solid grains.
**Where Venus, Earth and Mars formed**: more kinds of rock could condense. In the **asteroid belt** region, dark carbon-rich minerals and minerals holding a little water could condense.
**Beyond the frost line**: cold enough for **hydrogen compounds to freeze into ices**, alongside rock and metal.

steps.title: Where the frost line was and why it matters
bullets: The **frost line** marks the distance past which ices could condense. It sat **between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter**, in the outer asteroid belt, roughly **2.7 AU** out from the Sun.
**Inside** it, seeds were only **metal and rock**. **Beyond** it, seeds were **ice plus metal and rock**.
Rock and metal combined were outnumbered nearly three to one: hydrogen compounds were about **three times as abundant**. So beyond the frost line there was **much more solid material**.
That difference set the stage for two kinds of planets: small rocky ones inside and giant ones outside.

steps.title: Moving the frost line: what-if thinking
bullets: The frost line sits where the nebula's temperature drops to the temperature at which ices form.
If ices could form only at a **lower** temperature, the frost line would be **farther** out. If they could form at a higher temperature, it would be **closer**.
A **hotter, brighter young Sun** would warm the nebula farther out, pushing the frost line **outward**, so jovian planets would form farther away. A **cooler Sun** would pull it **inward**.
Gravity did not sort the materials: everything orbited together, and an orbit does not depend on an object's size or density. **Temperature** made the difference.

boxes.text: Why are the inner planets made of denser material? Near the Sun only metal and rock could become solid, even though hydrogen compounds were more plentiful. Far out, abundant ices joined the rock and metal, giving far more, and lighter, solid material.
Frost line between Mars and Jupiter: rocky worlds (and rocky asteroids) inside, icy worlds (and comets) outside. Colder needed = farther out.

It is a common misconception that the Sun's gravity pulled dense material inward or that spinning flung light material outward. The orbits do not depend on density; the cause was temperature. Cosmic Perspective puts the frost line at about 2.7 AU; the Ch8.2 pt1 slide only shows it on a diagram.

sections.title: Building the terrestrial planets by accretion

img.alt: A cat covered in white foam packing pieces that cling to its fur by static electricity.

steps.title: Tiny grains stick together
bullets: **Accretion** is the growth of small solid seeds into larger bodies by colliding and sticking.
The grains circled the young Sun along the same neat, circular paths as the gas around them, so neighbouring grains moved at almost the same speed and their collisions were just **gentle touches**.
Too small to attract each other by gravity, they stuck by **electrostatic forces**, the same **static electricity** that makes foam packing pieces cling to a cat's fur.
Small particles combined into larger ones, eventually becoming **planetesimals**, meaning pieces of planets.

img.alt: Three views of the inner solar system: many small bodies on crossing orbits, then fewer larger bodies, then just a few planets on separate orbits.

steps.title: Gravity takes over
bullets: Once planetesimals reached about **1 km across**, their **gravity** began to pull in other planetesimals.
Bigger bodies had more surface to hit and more gravity, so they grew fast. Some reached **hundreds of kilometres** within a few million years.
Over **tens of millions of years**, many small objects accreted into **just a few large ones**.

As they grew, gravitational encounters made their orbits **cross**. Collisions became faster and often **shattered** planetesimals rather than building them. Only the largest and luckiest survived to become **Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars**.

steps.title: Why the terrestrial planets are small and rocky
bullets: Closer to the Sun than the frost line, the only possible solids were **metal and rock**, and these made up just about **0.6%** of the nebula's mass.
So there was little solid material to build with, and the terrestrial planets ended up **small**.
Their gravity was too weak to capture much hydrogen and helium gas, so they stayed made of **metal and rock**.

Evidence: some **meteorites** that date from this time contain **flakes of metal mixed into rock**, just what condensation in the inner nebula predicts. Meteorites from the outer asteroid belt are rich in **carbon** and some hold **water**.

boxes.text: Why could gravity not build planets from the start? Microscopic grains have far too little mass to pull on each other. Only after electrostatic sticking built bodies about a kilometre across did gravity become strong enough to take over.
Accretion ladder: grains (static) → planetesimals (~1 km, gravity takes over) → a few planets (tens of millions of years).

Accretion is particles growing by colliding and sticking. Separating metal and rock from ices was condensation, an earlier stage, and Earth gaining water came later through impacts. Hydrogen and helium never bonded into solids. Ch8.2 pt1 slide 7 gives about 1 km as the size where gravity takes over.

sections.title: Building the jovian planets and their moons

steps.title: Big icy planetesimals capture gas
bullets: Beyond the frost line, **ices** joined rock and metal in the seeds. With so much more solid material, **larger planetesimals** could form there.
The early growth was the same as in the inner solar system: small grains of ice, rock and metal stuck together by **static electricity** and other non-gravitational forces.
Once the largest ice-rich planetesimals were massive enough, their **gravity** pulled in the surrounding **hydrogen and helium gas**.
The added gas made their gravity stronger still, so they captured even more gas. The jovian planets ended up **mostly hydrogen and helium**, far bigger than the icy seeds they grew from.

img.alt: A painting of the glowing solar nebula around the Sun with a magnified inset of a smaller spinning disk of gas around a forming jovian planet.

steps.title: Mini solar nebulae made the moons
bullets: Gas pulled toward a young jovian planet went through the same **heating, spinning and flattening** as the whole solar nebula.
Around each jovian planet formed its own **spinning disk**, rotating the same way the planet spun.
**Large moons** (and rings) formed by **condensation and accretion** inside these disks, like a solar system in miniature.

That is why most large jovian moons have **nearly circular orbits**, go the **same direction** as their planet rotates, and lie close to its **equatorial plane**. A young planet called PDS 70c has been seen inside its own dusty disk where moons may be forming.

boxes.text: Why did only the outer planets become giants? Only beyond the frost line was there enough solid material (ice as well as rock and metal) for planetesimals to become massive enough to pull in hydrogen and helium gas, which made up 98% of the nebula.
Jovian recipe: ice + rock + metal seed (static, then gravity) → big core → gravity captures H and He gas → spinning disk around it → regular moons.

The seeds of jovian planets did not grow by gravity from the start; like all seeds they first stuck by static electricity and other non-gravitational forces, and only a large planetesimal's gravity could then attract hydrogen and helium gas. Large jovian moons were not captured and are not pieces of a broken planet; they formed in disks around the planets. Ch8.2 pt1 slide 9 says the disks gave rise to 'moons and rings'.

sections.title: Clearing the nebula and slowing the Sun

steps.title: The leftover gas is blown away
bullets: Most of the nebula's hydrogen and helium never became part of any planet.
It was cleared away by the young Sun's **high-energy radiation** (ultraviolet and X-rays) and its **solar wind**, a stream of charged particles blowing outward in all directions.
Young stars have **much stronger winds** and give off much more high-energy radiation than older stars, so the young Sun's wind was **stronger than today's**.
Clearing **sealed the planets' compositions**: once the gas was gone, no planet could gather any more of it.

steps.title: What if the timing had been different?
bullets: **Gas stays longer**: the nebula would have kept cooling until ices could condense even in the inner solar system. The terrestrial planets could then have grown bigger and collected lots of ice, maybe hydrogen and helium gas too, which would have changed their basic nature.
**Gas blown away earlier**: the raw materials could have been swept off before the planets finished forming, leaving them smaller or unfinished.
Neither happened in our solar system, but both may happen around other stars. Radiation from hot neighbouring stars can also strip a young star's nebula.

img.alt: The young Sun inside the glowing nebula with purple magnetic field loops, and two arrows showing the magnetic field sweeping around faster than the nebula gas.

steps.title: Why the Sun spins slowly now
bullets: Conservation of angular momentum says the young Sun, holding most of the mass at the fast-spinning centre, should have rotated **very fast**. Today it turns only about **once a month**.
Angular momentum cannot disappear, but it can be **transferred and carried away**, like a spinning skater who grabs a partner and pushes him off.
The fast-spinning young Sun had a strong **magnetic field**. The field swept through the nebula faster than the gas orbited and **dragged the charged particles** along, which slowed the Sun.

When the gas was cleared into interstellar space, it **carried that angular momentum away**. Young stars spin fast with strong fields and winds; older stars spin slowly, so this seems to happen to almost all stars.

boxes.text: Why could clearing the nebula change everything? The planets' make-up depended on what was solid and what gas they could hold onto while the nebula was there. The moment the gas left, their basic compositions were fixed.
Young Sun: fast spin → strong magnetic field → strong wind and radiation → gas cleared, and the gas leaves carrying the Sun's spin.

The Sun did not slow down because spinning objects always slow down by themselves, and it is not a mystery for the nebular theory. Angular momentum was transferred to charged particles and carried away when the gas was cleared. Ch8.2 pt2 slide 1 credits the magnetic field; Cosmic Perspective adds the solar wind and high-energy radiation.

sections.title: Leftovers: asteroids, comets and the heavy bombardment

img.alt: Two photos: a grey, potato-shaped, cratered asteroid with a 5 km scale bar, and a comet with a glowing tail in the night sky above rocky peaks.

steps.title: Asteroids and comets are leftover planetesimals
bullets: **Asteroids** and **comets** are planetesimals that were never built into a planet. Some large ones count as **dwarf planets**.
**Asteroids** are rocky and metallic: leftovers from **inside the frost line**.
**Comets** are ice-rich: leftovers from **beyond the frost line**.
Evidence comes from meteorites, spacecraft visits and computer models. The theory even predicted that the **Kuiper belt** held comets, decades before anyone found one.

img.alt: A painting of the young, heavily cratered Earth and Moon, with a large impact throwing up a bright spray of debris on Earth.

steps.title: The heavy bombardment
bullets: The asteroids and comets left today are only a small fraction of the original leftovers. Some were flung into deep space; many **crashed into the planets and moons**.
Most of these collisions happened in the **first few hundred million years**, a period called the **heavy bombardment**, ending roughly 4 billion years ago.
Every world was pelted, and the impacts left **craters**. Most craters on the Moon date from this time.
A heavily cratered surface is therefore an **old surface** that has changed little since the bombardment; a smooth surface was reshaped later.

img.alt: Earth seen from space, with blue oceans, white clouds and the African continent.

steps.title: Where Earth's water came from
bullets: Earth formed **inside the frost line**, where it was too hot for water and other hydrogen compounds to condense, so its own planetesimals were dry.
Water and gases arrived with **icy planetesimals** that formed **farther from the Sun** and hit Earth while it was forming and during the heavy bombardment.

The ratio of **deuterium** (heavy hydrogen) to ordinary hydrogen suggests most of it came from planetesimals in the **outer asteroid belt**, just beyond the frost line. Some may have come from comets.
That means the water in our glasses and the air in our lungs were probably assembled **beyond the orbit of Mars**. Earth's water does not break the theory; impacts explain it.

boxes.text: Why are there leftovers at all? Accretion was never perfectly efficient. Many planetesimals avoided being swept up, and those that survived to the present are the asteroids and comets.
Asteroid = rocky leftover (inside the frost line). Comet = icy leftover (beyond it). Heavy bombardment = leftovers hitting planets in the first few hundred million years.

The heavy bombardment was impacts of leftover planetesimals on planets and moons, not planetesimals sticking together to make planets (that was accretion) and not planets hitting each other. Asteroids and comets did not condense long after the planets, are not wreckage of planets or moons and are not volcanic debris. Ch8.2 pt2 slide 4 says water 'may have' arrived on icy planetesimals.

sections.title: Exceptions: captured moons and giant impacts

img.alt: Close-ups of Mars's two small, lumpy moons Phobos and Deimos with kilometre scale bars, and Uranus with its rings running nearly up and down because the planet is tipped on its side.

steps.title: Captured moons
bullets: Some moons orbit the **wrong way** (opposite their planet's rotation) or on steeply **tilted** orbits. They did not form in the planet's disk.
They are probably **leftover planetesimals captured** into orbit.
Capture is hard: a passing body must **lose orbital energy**. Around young jovian planets, **friction with the thick gas** around them could slow passing planetesimals enough.

This works only for bodies up to a few kilometres across, and most small jovian moons are about that size. Mars's tiny moons **Phobos** (about 13 km) and **Deimos** (about 8 km) may be captured asteroids from a time when Mars had a thicker atmosphere.

steps.title: Giant impacts
bullets: Models suggest a few leftover planetesimals were as large as **Mars**. A collision with one could **tilt a planet's axis**, change its **spin**, or even shatter it.

A giant impact may have tipped **Uranus on its side** and could explain the **backward rotation** of Venus (and Uranus). Some scientists think Venus's thick atmosphere caused its slow, backward spin instead.
Mercury's huge metal core may be left over after an impact blasted away much of its rock. Pluto's moon **Charon** may have formed in an impact like the one that made our Moon.
Giant impacts are random, so we expect **a few exceptions**, which is exactly what we see. Most exceptions come from **collisions or close gravitational encounters** with leftover planetesimals.

boxes.text: Why do exceptions support the theory instead of breaking it? The early solar system was full of leftover planetesimals, some very large. With so many objects, a few rare collisions and captures were bound to happen, so a few oddballs are expected.
Wrong-way or tilted small moon → captured. Tipped or backward-spinning planet → giant impact. Big regular moon of a jovian planet → formed in its disk.

The exceptions are not explained by a passing star, by objects formed recently, or by objects captured from interstellar space. A few moons orbiting backward or planets spinning backward fit the nebular theory. Ch8.2 pt2 slide 5 says Mars's moons 'may be' captured and that giant impacts 'might' explain Uranus's tilt.

sourceNotes: Ch8.2 pt2 slide 5

sections.title: How our Moon formed: the giant impact

steps.title: Why the other ideas fail
bullets: **Capture** fails: our Moon is far too large compared with Earth to have been captured.
**Forming alongside Earth** fails: they would have been made from the same planetesimals and have about the same density, but the Moon's density is **much lower** than Earth's.
**Splitting off a fast-spinning Earth** (fission) needed an impossibly fast spin and a way to stop the piece flying off.
Moon rocks brought back by the **Apollo** missions ruled these out. The leading idea since 1974 is a **giant impact**.

img.alt: Three stages of an artist's sequence: a Mars-sized body smashes into the young Earth, molten debris is thrown into orbit, and a ring of leftover debris surrounds Earth as the young Moon gathers.

steps.title: The giant impact
bullets: A **Mars-sized planetesimal** hit the young Earth hard enough, and at the right angle, to blast material from Earth's **outer rocky layers** out into space.
Hours later Earth was molten and spinning very fast. Some debris fell back; the rest formed a ring in orbit.
Within the ring the debris **accreted into the Moon**, which was nearly complete in less than a thousand years.
The Moon formed close to Earth. Over billions of years tides have slowed Earth's spin and moved the Moon farther out.

steps.title: Evidence for the giant impact
bullets: **Computer simulations** of a collision with a Mars-sized body can reproduce today's Earth-Moon system.

The Moon's overall composition is very **similar to Earth's outer layers** (mantle and crust), as expected if it came from them. It has very **little metal**, because the material came from outside Earth's metal core.
Moon samples lack **volatile** substances such as **water, sodium and zinc**, which the heat of the impact would have turned to gas so they never joined the Moon.
The oldest Moon rocks are about **4.4 billion years** old, so the impact happened **more than 4.4 billion years ago**. We may never prove it directly, but it is very likely correct.

boxes.text: Why does a missing-volatiles clue matter? Only something extremely hot could boil away water, sodium and zinc. A gentle formation alongside Earth would have kept them; a giant impact would have vaporized them.
Four clues for the giant impact: it works in simulations, it matches Earth's outer layers, it lost the easily boiled substances, and it has little metal.

The Moon being geologically quiet today says nothing about how it formed; it is due to its small size, which let it cool fast. The same goes for the Moon always showing us the same face. The giant impact hypothesis says the Moon came from Earth's mantle and crust, not that two asteroids collided or that a once Earth-sized Moon was mostly blasted away. Ch8.2 pt2 slide 7 lists water, sodium and zinc as missing volatiles.

sourceNotes: Ch8.2 pt2 slides 6-7

sections.title: Putting it together: an orderly start and chancy details

img.alt: A top-to-bottom sequence: a cloud collapses into a flat disk, solid grains condense, planetesimals grow and gather, and the final system of planets orbits the Sun.

steps.title: The whole story in order
bullets: A large interstellar cloud, enriched by earlier stars, **collapses under gravity**.
It **heats up, spins faster and flattens** into a spinning disk with the young Sun at the centre.
Metal and rock **condense** everywhere cool enough; ices condense only **beyond the frost line**.
Seeds **accrete** into planetesimals: terrestrial planets inside the frost line; big icy cores that capture **hydrogen and helium** outside it, with moons forming in their disks.
The **solar wind clears** the leftover gas. **Leftovers** become asteroids and comets, and many hit the planets during the **heavy bombardment**.

steps.title: What was inevitable and what was luck
bullets: The early stages, making a **spinning disk**, **condensation** and the first steps of **accretion**, were orderly and **inevitable**. So two types of planets, inner rocky and outer giant, were bound to form.
The later stages, crossing orbits, **giant impacts** and planets nudging each other's orbits, were **random**. The details of each planet could easily have been different.
No other planetary system is likely to be exactly like ours. Planets can even **migrate** inward or outward from where they formed.
The solar system formed about **4.5 billion years ago**, about a third of the age of the universe.

boxes.text: Why can we say two planet types were inevitable? They follow directly from physics that acts the same in every collapsing cloud: heating makes the centre hot, so a frost line must exist, with rocky seeds inside and icy seeds outside.
Orderly: disk, condensation, early accretion. Chance: giant impacts, captures, exact orbits. Patterns are predicted; exceptions are luck.

Earth's large Moon, Uranus's tilt and Venus's backward spin would probably be different if the solar system formed again, but rocky inner planets and giant outer planets would not. Ch8.2 pt2 slide 9 gives the age as about 4.5 billion years; radiometric dating (Cosmic Perspective 8.3) is not on the slides and is left out of this unit.
