cards.back: The scientific theory that a giant interstellar cloud of gas and dust, the solar nebula, underwent gravitational collapse and formed the solar system, with the Sun at the centre and the planets in a spinning disk around it. It explains all four major features of the solar system.
cards.short: Solar system formed from a collapsing gas cloud

cards.back: A discarded idea that the planets formed from blobs of gas pulled out of the Sun by a near-collision with another star. It could not explain the planets' orbital motions or the two planet types, and it would make planetary systems extremely rare.
cards.short: Planets as debris from a passing star (rejected)

cards.back: The interstellar cloud of gas and dust from which the Sun and planets formed. By mass it was about 98% hydrogen and helium and 2% everything else.
cards.short: The cloud the solar system formed from

cards.back: The facts a formation theory must explain: orderly motions (same direction, same plane), two types of planets, huge numbers of asteroids and comets, and a few exceptions such as Uranus's tilt and Earth's large Moon.
cards.short: Motions, two planet types, small bodies, exceptions

cards.back: The loop in which stars form from interstellar clouds, make heavier elements by fusion, and return that material to space when they die (as a planetary nebula or a supernova), enriching the gas that forms the next stars.
cards.short: Stars make elements and return them to space

cards.back: In astronomy, every element other than hydrogen and helium. The Big Bang made almost none; they were made in stars. They were only about 2% of the solar nebula's mass, yet they built every rocky world.
cards.short: Everything besides hydrogen and helium

cards.back: The first stars after the Big Bang, made from gas that was only hydrogen and helium. With nothing that could condense into solid grains, they could not have had planets, asteroids or comets.
cards.short: Hydrogen-and-helium-only stars with no planets
cards.src: Ch8.1 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 8.1 (Think About It)

cards.back: The likely outside push that started the solar nebula's collapse: a shock wave from a nearby exploding star. After the trigger, gravity kept the collapse going.
cards.short: A shock wave that may have started the collapse
cards.src: Ch8.2 pt1 slide 2; Cosmic Perspective 8.2 and Special Topic

cards.back: The shrinking of a gas cloud under its own gravity. Because the mass stays the same while the cloud shrinks, gravity grows stronger and the collapse speeds up.
cards.short: A cloud shrinking under its own gravity

cards.back: The warming of a shrinking cloud as gravitational potential energy turns into kinetic energy of infalling gas and then into thermal energy when particles collide. It is conservation of energy at work.
cards.short: Shrinking cloud heats up (energy conserved)

cards.back: The faster rotation of the solar nebula as it shrank, required by conservation of angular momentum, like a skater pulling in her arms. It kept most material orbiting in a disk instead of falling into the Sun.
cards.short: Shrinking cloud spins faster (angular momentum)

cards.back: The squashing of a rotating, collapsing cloud into a disk. Colliding clumps average out their random motions, leaving only the overall spin, and orbits become more circular.
cards.short: Collisions turn a cloud into a flat disk

cards.back: A flattened, spinning disk of gas and dust around a young star, in which planets can form. Examples are seen in the Orion Nebula and around Beta Pictoris.
cards.short: Disk around a young star where planets form

cards.back: The young Sun forming at the dense, hot centre of the collapsing solar nebula, before the leftover gas was cleared.
cards.short: The Sun while it was still forming

cards.back: Molecules such as water, methane and ammonia. They were about 1.4% of the solar nebula's mass and froze into ices only below about 150 K, so only beyond the frost line.
cards.short: Water, methane, ammonia: ices below about 150 K

cards.back: Various minerals, about 0.4% of the solar nebula's mass, which condense into solid grains below about 500 to 1300 K depending on the mineral.
cards.short: Minerals: 0.4%, solid below 500 to 1300 K

cards.back: Iron, nickel and aluminum: the scarcest ingredient (about 0.2% of the mass) but the first to condense, below about 1000 to 1600 K.
cards.short: Iron, nickel, aluminum: 0.2%, condense first

cards.back: The formation of solid (or liquid) particles from a gas when it is cool enough, like snowflakes forming in a cloud. In the solar nebula it made the tiny solid seeds of the planets.
cards.short: Solid grains forming out of a gas

cards.back: The distance from the young Sun past which it was cold enough that hydrogen compounds could condense into ices. It lay between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, about 2.7 AU from the Sun.
cards.short: Where ices could start to form (about 2.7 AU)

cards.back: The growth of small solid particles into larger bodies by colliding and sticking together, first by static electricity and then, once large enough, by gravity.
cards.short: Growth by colliding and sticking

cards.back: A small body, from boulder size up to hundreds of kilometres, built by accretion in the solar nebula. The name means piece of a planet. Planetesimals merged to make planets; the leftovers are asteroids and comets.
cards.short: A piece of a planet built by accretion

cards.back: The way microscopic grains stuck together before they were big enough to attract each other by gravity: static electricity, like foam pieces clinging to a cat's fur.
cards.short: Static electricity holding tiny grains together

cards.back: A rock that has fallen to Earth from space. Some date from the birth of the solar system and contain metal flakes mixed with rock, as the nebular theory predicts for the inner nebula.
cards.short: A space rock that reached the ground

cards.back: The last stage of jovian planet growth: a large ice-rich planetesimal's gravity pulls in hydrogen and helium gas from the nebula, which strengthens its gravity so it captures still more.
cards.short: Big icy cores pulling in hydrogen and helium

cards.back: A spinning disk of gas and dust around a forming jovian planet, a small copy of the solar nebula. Large regular moons and rings formed in these disks.
cards.short: Disk around a young giant planet where moons form

cards.back: A moon that formed in its planet's disk, so it has a nearly circular orbit in the direction of the planet's rotation, close to its equator. Most large jovian moons are regular.
cards.short: Moon born in its planet's disk

cards.back: A moon that was once a leftover planetesimal orbiting the Sun and was trapped by a planet, for example after friction with the gas around a young jovian planet. It may orbit backward or on a tilted orbit.
cards.short: Leftover planetesimal trapped in orbit

cards.back: Mars's two small, lumpy moons, about 13 km and 8 km across. They may be captured asteroids rather than moons that formed around Mars.
cards.short: Mars's tiny moons, possibly captured

cards.back: Charged particles (protons and electrons, for example) streaming away from the Sun in every direction. The young Sun's wind was much stronger than today's.
cards.short: Charged particles streaming from the Sun

cards.back: The removal of the leftover hydrogen and helium gas by the young Sun's strong solar wind and high-energy radiation. It fixed the planets' compositions and carried away the Sun's angular momentum.
cards.short: Leftover gas blown out of the solar system

cards.back: How the young Sun slowed down: its magnetic field swept through the nebula faster than the gas orbited, dragging charged particles and handing them angular momentum, which left the solar system when the gas was cleared.
cards.short: Sun's field passed its spin to the nebula gas

cards.back: Planetesimals that never became part of a planet: rocky asteroids from inside the frost line and icy comets from beyond it. Many others hit the planets or were flung into deep space.
cards.short: Asteroids and comets

cards.back: An early era, lasting a few hundred million years after the solar system formed and ending roughly 4 billion years ago, when leftover planetesimals often slammed into planets and moons and made most of the craters we see.
cards.short: Early era of frequent impacts

cards.back: A bowl-shaped scar left when an asteroid or comet hits a solid surface. A surface crowded with craters is old, dating back to the heavy bombardment.
cards.short: Scar left by an impact

cards.back: How Earth got water although it formed where water could not condense: icy planetesimals from beyond the frost line, mostly from the outer asteroid belt, hit the young Earth.
cards.short: Icy planetesimals brought Earth its water

cards.back: Heavy hydrogen, with a neutron in its nucleus. Its ratio to ordinary hydrogen in Earth's water matches planetesimals from the outer asteroid belt, pointing to where the water came from.
cards.short: Heavy hydrogen used to trace water's origin

cards.back: A collision between a planet and a very large leftover planetesimal, which can tilt the planet's axis, change its spin or blast away its outer layers.
cards.short: A planet-scale collision

cards.back: The leading idea for our Moon's origin: a Mars-sized planetesimal struck the young Earth, throwing material from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it accreted into the Moon more than 4.4 billion years ago.
cards.short: Moon made from debris of a Mars-sized impact

cards.back: Substances that turn to gas easily, such as water, sodium and zinc. Moon samples have very few of them, as expected if the heat of a giant impact boiled them away.
cards.short: Easily vaporized substances (water, sodium, zinc)

cards.back: Features that break the solar system's general patterns, such as Uranus's extreme tilt, the backward rotations of Venus and Uranus, captured moons and Earth's large Moon. Most are explained by giant impacts, captures or close encounters.
cards.short: Oddities explained by impacts and captures

cards.back: Uranus's axis is tipped almost onto its side, an exception to the rules. A giant impact with a large planetesimal may have knocked it over.
cards.short: Tipped on its side, maybe by a giant impact

cards.back: About 4.5 billion years: the planets formed within roughly the first 50 million years after accretion began, about a third of the age of the universe.
cards.short: About 4.5 billion years

cards.back: Gravitational potential energy became kinetic energy of falling gas; collisions turned it into heat, and much of it escaped as radiation.
cards.short: Potential to kinetic to heat

cards.back: Nebula collapses, planetesimals accrete, leftover gas is cleared, then the heavy bombardment ends a few hundred million years later.
cards.short: Collapse, accrete, clear, bombardment ends

quiz.q: Which of these would a successful theory of how the solar system formed NOT be expected to explain?
options: Why the planets orbit in the same direction and nearly the same plane
The exact number of moons that each planet has
Why there are small rocky planets near the Sun and giant planets farther out
Why there are huge numbers of asteroids and comets
Why a few objects, such as Uranus, break the general patterns
quiz.why: A formation theory has to explain four major features: orderly motions, two types of planets, many asteroids and comets, and the existence of a few exceptions. The exact moon count of each planet depends on chance events such as captures and impacts, so no theory is expected to predict it. The other four options are the four features themselves.

quiz.q: Thousands of planetary systems have now been found around other stars. Why does this count against the close encounter hypothesis but in favour of the nebular theory?
options: The other systems all contain exactly the same planets as ours
Close encounters can only make jovian planets, and the systems found are all terrestrial
The nebular theory says planets form only around stars that have no neighbours
Close encounters would make every star have planets, which is too many
Near-collisions between stars are so rare that they could not make planets common, while the nebular theory makes planets a normal by-product of star birth
quiz.why: Stars are so far apart that a near-collision is extremely unlikely, so if planets came from such accidents they would be very rare. The nebular theory says disks and planets form whenever stars form, so it predicts many planetary systems, which is what we see. Other systems are not copies of ours, and close encounters would make planets rare, not common.

quiz.q: Where did most of the iron now in Earth's core originally come from?
options: It was made in the Big Bang
It was made by nuclear fusion in the young Sun's core
It was made inside earlier generations of stars and released when they died
It was produced by radioactive decay inside the young Earth
It condensed directly from hydrogen in the solar nebula
quiz.why: The Big Bang made almost only hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements such as iron were made in earlier stars and returned to space when those stars died, then mixed into the solar nebula. The young Sun's fusion stays inside the Sun, radioactive decay breaks heavy nuclei down rather than building iron, and hydrogen cannot condense into iron.

quiz.q: A sample of solar nebula material has a mass of 1000 kg. About how much of it is rock?
options: About 4 kg
About 2 kg
About 14 kg
About 20 kg
About 980 kg
quiz.why: Rock was about 0.4% of the nebula's mass, and 0.4% of 1000 kg is 4 kg. About 2 kg would be the metal (0.2%), 14 kg the hydrogen compounds (1.4%), 20 kg all the heavy materials together (2%), and 980 kg the hydrogen and helium gas (98%).

quiz.q: Spectra show that old stars contain a smaller share of heavy elements than young stars. What does this support?
options: Old stars have destroyed their heavy elements by fusion
Heavy elements sink to the centres of old stars, where we cannot see them
Young stars make heavy elements much faster than old stars did
Galactic recycling has slowly enriched the gas in the galaxy with heavy elements over time
Heavy elements escape from stars as they grow old
quiz.why: Old stars formed early, before many generations of stars had added heavy elements to interstellar gas. Young stars formed later from enriched gas. This is just what galactic recycling predicts. The other options invent processes that would not explain why the difference depends on when the star formed.

quiz.q: Imagine a star system forming today from a cloud with twice the usual share of heavy elements (4% instead of 2%). Based on the nebular theory, what is the most reasonable expectation?
options: No planets could form, because the extra elements would stop the collapse
More solid material could condense, so planetesimals and planets could grow larger or more easily
Only jovian planets could form
The planets would orbit in random planes
The cloud could not form a star at its centre
quiz.why: Only the heavy elements (rock, metal and hydrogen compounds) can become solid seeds, so a richer cloud gives more raw material for accretion. Nothing in the theory says extra heavy elements stop collapse, ruin the disk's orderly spin, or prevent a central star; the gas is still mostly hydrogen and helium.
quiz.source: Ch8.1 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 8.1-8.2 (reasoning from the 98% / 2% composition)

quiz.q: Once the collapse of the solar nebula had started, what kept it going?
options: The supernova shock wave, which kept pushing for millions of years
Magnetic attraction between iron grains
Pressure from the light of the young Sun
The cloud's rotation, which pulled material inward
Gravity, which grew stronger as the cloud shrank
quiz.why: A shock wave may have started the collapse, but gravity kept it going: the mass stayed the same while the cloud got smaller, so gravity grew stronger. A shock wave is a brief push, iron grains were a tiny fraction of the cloud, light pushes outward, and rotation resists collapse rather than causing it.

quiz.q: Where did the heat of the collapsing solar nebula come from?
options: Nuclear fusion throughout the cloud
Friction between the disk and the young Sun's magnetic field
Gravitational potential energy became kinetic energy of falling gas, which collisions turned into thermal energy
Radioactive decay of elements made in the Big Bang
Starlight absorbed from neighbouring stars
quiz.why: As gas fell inward it lost gravitational potential energy and gained speed; collisions then turned that motion into random thermal motion, so the cloud heated up. This is conservation of energy. Fusion began only in the Sun's core, the magnetic drag came later and slowed the Sun, the Big Bang made almost no radioactive elements, and starlight cannot explain heat concentrated at the centre.

quiz.q: Why do astronomers search for infrared light from clouds where stars are forming, and what has the search found?
options: A collapsing cloud heats up, and warm gas gives off thermal radiation mostly in the infrared; such radiation is seen from many star-forming clouds
Infrared light shows that the clouds are cooling as they collapse
Infrared is the only light that can show a cloud's rotation
Infrared light is produced by the supernova that triggers the collapse
Infrared shows that the clouds contain no dust
quiz.why: The theory predicts that collapsing clouds heat up, and warm (but not very hot) objects emit thermal radiation mainly in the infrared. Infrared radiation has been detected from many nebulae where stars appear to be forming, which supports the theory. The clouds heat rather than cool, rotation is measured with Doppler shifts, and the clouds clearly contain dust.

quiz.q: What was the main reason that not all of the solar nebula fell into the Sun?
options: Pressure from the hot centre blew the outer material away
The outer material was too cold to be pulled in by gravity
The young Sun's magnetic field held the material out
The cloud's rotation sped up as it shrank, so much material kept orbiting in a spread-out disk
The Sun's gravity was switched off until it began fusion
quiz.why: Conservation of angular momentum made the shrinking cloud spin faster, and fast-orbiting material cannot fall straight in, so it formed a disk. The more angular momentum, the more spread out the result. Temperature does not stop gravity, the magnetic field acted later on the gas, and gravity never switches off.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slides 2 and 4; Cosmic Perspective 8.2

quiz.q: Why did the spinning solar nebula end up flat instead of staying a smaller ball?
options: Gravity pulls only toward the equator of a cloud
Colliding clumps averaged out their random motions, leaving only the overall spin in one plane
The young Sun's light pushed material into a thin layer
Spinning flung all the gas outward equally in every direction
The original cloud happened to be shaped like a disk
quiz.why: Clumps moving in random directions collided and merged, each taking the average motion. Up-and-down motions cancelled, but the overall spin could not, so the cloud became a rotating disk. Gravity pulls in all directions (which is why the Sun is round), light pressure did not shape the disk, spinning does not push equally in all directions, and the disk shape was not luck.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT explained by the planets forming in a spinning, flattened disk?
options: The planets orbit in nearly the same plane
The planets orbit in the same direction as the Sun rotates
Planetary orbits are nearly circular
Most planets rotate in the same direction as they orbit
Venus rotates backward
quiz.why: Venus's backward rotation is an exception to the rules, probably caused by a giant impact or by its thick atmosphere, not by the disk. The disk explains the common plane, the shared direction of the Sun's spin and the planets' orbits, the nearly circular orbits (collisions circularized them) and why most planets spin the same way.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slide 4 and Ch8.2 pt2 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 8.2

quiz.q: Which pairing of a law with what it predicts for a shrinking gas cloud is correct?
options: Conservation of energy: it spins faster; conservation of angular momentum: it heats up
Conservation of energy: it cools off; conservation of angular momentum: it spins slower
Conservation of energy: it heats up; conservation of angular momentum: it spins faster
Conservation of energy: it stops shrinking; conservation of angular momentum: it flattens
Both laws predict only that it keeps shrinking
quiz.why: Energy conservation turns gravitational potential energy into thermal energy, so the cloud heats up. Angular momentum conservation means a smaller cloud must spin faster, like a skater pulling in her arms. The swapped pair mixes up the two laws, cooling and spinning slower are the opposite of what happens, and flattening comes from collisions.

quiz.q: Imagine a cloud that somehow had exactly zero overall rotation when it began to collapse. What would the nebular theory predict?
options: Almost all of the material would fall straight into the centre, leaving little or no disk to build planets
It would still form a wide, flat disk exactly like ours
It would spin faster and faster as it shrank
It would form planets that orbit in random planes around a star
It would not heat up as it collapsed
quiz.why: Rotation is what holds material out in a disk: the more angular momentum, the more spread out the cloud ends up. With none, nothing would stop the gas falling straight in, so there would be little or no disk. Zero rotation cannot speed up, it would still heat up because heating comes from energy conservation, and without a disk there is nothing to make planets. In practice the random motions of a real cloud almost never cancel exactly.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slides 2 and 4; Cosmic Perspective 8.2 (reasoning)

quiz.q: A region of the solar nebula had a temperature of about 1300 K. What was solid there?
options: Ice, rock and metal grains
Nothing at all; every ingredient was gas
Rock but no metal
Tiny grains of metal and a little of the most heat-resistant rock, while almost all of the mass stayed gas
Grains of frozen hydrogen and helium
quiz.why: Metals condense below about 1000 to 1600 K, so they were solid at 1300 K; rock condenses below 500 to 1300 K, so only its toughest minerals could just form. Hydrogen compounds need below about 150 K, and hydrogen and helium never condense. Since 98% of the mass is hydrogen and helium, nearly everything stayed gas.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 8.2 (Table 8.1, Think About It)

quiz.q: A region of the solar nebula had a temperature of about 100 K. Where was it, and what was solid there?
options: Inside the frost line; only metal grains
Beyond the frost line; grains of ice as well as rock and metal
Inside the frost line; ice, rock and metal
Beyond the frost line; only rock and metal, because ice needs higher temperatures
Near the young Sun; nothing solid
quiz.why: 100 K is colder than the roughly 150 K needed for hydrogen compounds to freeze, so the region was beyond the frost line, farther from the Sun, and ices could form along with rock and metal. The inner nebula was much warmer, and ices form at low, not high, temperatures.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 8.2 (Table 8.1, Think About It)

quiz.q: Why did the planets beyond the frost line grow so much larger than the terrestrial planets?
options: The Sun's gravity pushed light gas outward to where they were forming
The outer nebula was much denser than the inner nebula
The outer part of the disk spun faster, gathering material more quickly
They formed much earlier, before the Sun had begun to shine
Ices could condense there, and hydrogen compounds were about three times as abundant as rock and metal combined, so planetesimals grew big enough to capture hydrogen and helium gas
quiz.why: Beyond the frost line, abundant ices joined rock and metal, so there was far more solid material and the planetesimals became massive enough for their gravity to pull in the hydrogen and helium gas. Gravity does not sort material by weight, the inner nebula was denser, the outer disk orbits more slowly, and timing is not the reason.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slides 5 and 8; Cosmic Perspective 8.2

quiz.q: A student says the inner planets are dense because the Sun's gravity pulled heavy materials inward while light gas drifted out. What is wrong with this idea?
options: Nothing is wrong; this is what the nebular theory says
The Sun's gravity actually pushed heavy materials outward
All the materials orbited the Sun together, and an orbit does not depend on an object's size or density; temperature decided what became solid
The Sun had no gravity until fusion began
Heavy materials were only made after the planets had formed
quiz.why: The Sun's gravity acts on every particle in the same way regardless of its density, so it cannot sort materials. What differed was temperature: near the Sun only metal and rock could condense, while ices could form only far out. Gravity never pushes outward, it existed from the start, and the heavy elements were already in the nebula.
quiz.source: Ch8.2 pt1 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 8.2 (Common Misconceptions)

quiz.q: Suppose the young Sun had been dimmer and cooler than it really was. What would the nebular theory predict?
options: The frost line would have been closer to the Sun, so icy planetesimals and jovian planets could have formed nearer the Sun
The frost line would have been farther from the Sun
There would have been no frost line at all
Terrestrial planets would have formed beyond the jovian planets
The nebula would not have flattened into a disk
quiz.why: A dimmer Sun warms the nebula less, so the temperature low enough for ices is reached closer in, moving the frost line inward and letting jovian planets form nearer the Sun. A brighter Sun would push it outward instead. A frost line still exists wherever the disk gets cold enough, the planet order would not reverse, and flattening does not depend on the Sun's brightness.

quiz.q: In the earliest stage of accretion, what made microscopic grains stick together?
options: Their mutual gravity
Magnetism in iron grains only
Melting and welding by the Sun's heat
Electrostatic forces (static electricity)
Nuclear forces between their atoms
quiz.why: Grains moved gently alongside each other and stuck by static electricity, the same force that makes foam packing cling to a cat. Their gravity was far too weak until they reached about a kilometre across, most grains were not magnetic, melting would have destroyed them, and nuclear forces act only inside nuclei.

quiz.q: At about what size could a planetesimal start pulling in other planetesimals by its gravity?
options: About 1 millimetre across
About 1 kilometre across
About 1 metre across
About 1000 kilometres across
Only once it was as big as Earth
quiz.why: Once planetesimals reached roughly a kilometre across, their gravity was strong enough to attract other planetesimals, and growth sped up. Millimetre or metre-sized bodies have far too little mass, and gravity was already working long before bodies reached 1000 km or Earth size.

quiz.q: The inner solar system once held many large planetesimals, yet only four terrestrial planets exist today. Why?
options: The solar wind blew away all but four of them
The Sun's gravity swallowed all but four
Four is the number of rock and metal types that condensed
They were captured as moons by the jovian planets
Their orbits came to cross, so collisions grew faster and often shattered planetesimals; only the largest and luckiest survived and swept up the rest
quiz.why: Gravitational encounters altered the planetesimals' orbits so that they crossed. Faster collisions shattered many bodies instead of building them, and it took size plus luck for one to keep growing; four survivors became Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. The solar wind cleared gas, not large solid bodies, and the other options have no basis.

quiz.q: Why did the terrestrial planets end up relatively small?
options: The Sun's gravity tore pieces off them
They formed after most of the material had been used up by the jovian planets
Only metal and rock could be solid in the inner nebula, and together they were less than 1% of its mass
The inner nebula contained no hydrogen or helium gas
Inner planetesimals could not stick together
quiz.why: Inside the frost line only metal (0.2%) and rock (0.4%) could condense, so there was very little solid material. The planets never grew large enough to capture much gas before the nebula was cleared. The Sun did not break them apart, the timing was not the issue, there was plenty of gas in the inner nebula, and inner planetesimals stuck together just as outer ones did.

quiz.q: Some very old meteorites contain shiny flakes of metal mixed in with rocky minerals. What does this support?
options: Metal and rock condensed as separate tiny solid grains in the inner solar nebula, as the nebular theory predicts
The meteorites came from the core of a destroyed planet
Metals condensed only beyond the frost line
Meteorites formed long after the planets
Ice and rock condensed together near the Sun
quiz.why: Metal and rock condense at different high temperatures, so in the inner nebula both formed small grains that were then stuck together, exactly as seen. A planet's core would be nearly all metal, metals condensed near the Sun, these meteorites date from the solar system's birth, and ice could not condense near the Sun.

quiz.q: Most large moons of Jupiter and Saturn orbit in nearly circular paths, in the direction their planet rotates, near its equator. What explains this pattern?
options: The moons were captured one by one from the asteroid belt
The moons are pieces that broke off the planets as they spun
The Sun's gravity lined the moons up with the planets' equators
Each giant planet had its own spinning disk of gas and dust, and the moons formed in it like a small solar system
They were formed by a giant impact on each planet
quiz.why: Gas drawn toward a young jovian planet heated, spun up and flattened into a disk, just like the solar nebula, so moons that accreted there inherited its orderly motion. Captured moons would have random directions and tilts, planets did not fling off moons, the Sun's gravity does not align moon orbits, and giant impacts explain exceptions, not a regular pattern.

quiz.q: A jovian planet has a small moon, about 3 km across, that orbits opposite to the planet's rotation on a steeply tilted orbit. How did it most likely become a moon?
options: It formed in the planet's spinning disk
It was a leftover planetesimal that lost orbital energy to friction with gas around the young planet and was captured
It broke off the planet during a giant impact
It formed from the planet's rings
It condensed after the nebula was cleared
quiz.why: A backward, tilted orbit cannot come from the planet's disk, which would give a forward, equatorial orbit. Capture through drag in the thick gas around a young jovian planet works for bodies up to a few kilometres across, which fits this moon's size. The other options would not give a random direction and tilt.

quiz.q: What if the young Sun's wind had blown away the nebula's gas much EARLIER than it did?
options: The terrestrial planets would have become gas giants
The frost line would have moved inside Mercury's orbit
The Sun would be spinning much faster today
Nothing would change, because the planets were already complete
The raw materials might have been swept away before the planets finished forming, leaving smaller or unfinished planets
quiz.why: Clearing ends the planets' chance to gather material. If it had happened too early, material could have been removed before accretion and gas capture were done, so the planets, especially the jovian ones, would have been smaller. Becoming gas giants would need more time, not less; the frost line depends on temperature; an earlier clearing would still carry away the Sun's angular momentum.

quiz.q: Which observation of other stars supports the idea that the young Sun spun fast and was slowed by its magnetic field?
options: Old stars rotate faster than young stars
Young stars have no magnetic fields
Young stars nearly all rotate rapidly and have strong magnetic fields and winds, while older stars almost all rotate slowly
Every star spins at the same rate throughout its life
Young stars have no disks of gas around them
quiz.why: If stars generally lose angular momentum by transferring it to charged particles in their disks, which are later blown away, then young stars should spin fast and old stars slowly, which is what we see. The other options either contradict the observations or would give no reason for the Sun to slow down.

quiz.q: A newly found small body is a mix of ice and rocky dust. According to the nebular theory, where did it most likely form?
options: Beyond the frost line, as an icy leftover planetesimal (a comet)
Inside the frost line, as a rocky leftover planetesimal (an asteroid)
In the Sun's outer layers, ejected by the solar wind
From a volcano on one of the terrestrial planets
Long after the planets, from gas left in the inner solar system
quiz.why: Ice can be part of a solid body only if it formed where the nebula was cold enough, beyond the frost line, so this is a comet. Asteroids from inside the frost line are rock and metal. The Sun does not throw out solid icy bodies, volcanoes do not make comets, and leftovers formed with the planets, not long after.

quiz.q: One region of the Moon is crowded with overlapping craters, while another has very few. What does the heavily cratered region most likely tell us?
options: It is the youngest part of the Moon's surface
It was hit recently by a swarm of asteroids
It faces away from Earth, so asteroids only hit that side
Its surface dates from the heavy bombardment, early in the solar system's history, and has changed little since
Craters form only on high ground
quiz.why: Most impacts happened during the heavy bombardment in the first few hundred million years, so a surface covered with craters must be very old and undisturbed since then. A smooth region was resurfaced later, for example by lava. Impacts are rare today, both sides of the Moon were hit, and craters form on any solid ground.

quiz.q: Earth formed where it was too warm for water to condense, yet it has oceans. What does current evidence suggest?
options: The water condensed directly at Earth's distance as the nebula cooled
Most of the water came from water-bearing planetesimals of the outer asteroid belt, which formed beyond the frost line and hit the young Earth
The water was made by chemical reactions in Earth's metal core
The water was captured from the solar wind
The water shows that the nebular theory is wrong
quiz.why: Ratios of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen point to planetesimals from the outer asteroid belt, just beyond the frost line, which held some ice; comets may have added some too. Water never condensed near Earth's orbit, the core is metal, the solar wind carries no oceans' worth of water, and impacts explain the water within the theory.

quiz.q: Which observation would be hardest to explain if the Moon had formed alongside Earth from the same planetesimals?
options: The Moon orbits in roughly the same direction that Earth spins
The Moon is covered with craters
The Moon has no thick atmosphere
The Moon is round
The Moon's average density is much lower than Earth's
quiz.why: Bodies formed together from the same kind of planetesimals should have about the same composition and density, but the Moon's density is much lower, which points to a different origin. The direction of orbit, craters from the bombardment, the lack of an atmosphere (it is small) and its round shape (gravity) fit any idea.

quiz.q: The oldest Moon rocks are about 4.4 billion years old. What does this tell us about the giant impact that formed the Moon?
options: It happened less than 4.4 billion years ago
It happened exactly 4.4 billion years ago
It happened more than 4.4 billion years ago
It tells us nothing about when the impact happened
It happened before the Sun had formed
quiz.why: The Moon had to exist before any rock on it could solidify, so the impact that made it must be older than its oldest rocks. It cannot be younger than the rocks, rocks need not have formed at the exact moment of impact, and the planets formed after the Sun.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT support the giant impact hypothesis for our Moon?
options: The Moon always keeps the same face toward Earth
Moon samples have very few volatile substances such as water and zinc
The Moon's composition is similar to Earth's outer rocky layers
Computer simulations of a Mars-sized impact can produce an Earth-Moon system like ours
The Moon contains very little metal
quiz.why: Keeping one face toward Earth is synchronous rotation, caused later by tides, and would happen however the Moon formed. The missing volatiles (boiled off by the heat), the match with Earth's mantle and crust, the successful simulations and the lack of metal (the material came from outside Earth's core) all support the giant impact.

quiz.q: Why does the nebular theory expect the solar system to have a few exceptions to its general patterns?
options: A star passed close to the Sun after the planets formed
Some planets formed recently from captured interstellar gas
The laws of physics worked differently in the young solar system
The early solar system held many leftover planetesimals, some very large, so a few random collisions and captures were bound to happen
Exceptions show that the nebular theory is mostly wrong
quiz.why: With so many leftover planetesimals, a few giant impacts and captures were unavoidable, and these explain features such as Uranus's tilt, Venus's backward spin, captured moons and our Moon. No passing star or recent formation is needed, physics did not change, and exceptions of this kind fit the theory rather than break it.

quiz.q: If the solar system could form again from the same cloud, which feature would most likely turn out the same?
options: Earth having a large Moon
Rocky planets close to the Sun and giant planets farther out
Uranus being tipped on its side
Venus rotating backward
Exactly four terrestrial planets in today's orbits
quiz.why: The two types of planets follow from orderly physics: heating creates a frost line, with rocky seeds inside and icy seeds outside. The Moon, Uranus's tilt and Venus's spin came from random giant impacts, and the exact number and orbits of the survivors depended on chance collisions, so those would probably differ.

quiz.q: Which of the following observations of an extrasolar planet system would be inconsistent with what we expect from the nebular theory of solar system formation?
options: a system in which some planets have small moons orbiting in a direction opposite to the planet's rotation
a system which has two terrestrial planets close in and two jovian planets farther out
a system in which all the planets orbit in completely different planes
a system in which some planets rotate in a direction opposite to their orbits
quiz.why: The nebular theory says planets form in a flat disk made when the collapsing cloud flattened, so planets should orbit in nearly the same plane. A system where every planet orbits in a completely different plane would contradict that. The other systems fit the theory: some small moons can be captured planetesimals orbiting the wrong way, rocky planets inside and gas giants outside is the pattern the frost line predicts, and a planet spinning against its orbit can come from a giant impact.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT evidence against the close encounter hypothesis of star system formation?
options: We observe the planets all orbiting in the same direction around the Sun.
The vast majority of stars have orbiting planets.
The composition of the Sun is very different from that of the planets.
We observe stars forming from protoplanetary disks in nebulae.
quiz.why: Three of the statements are things the close encounter idea cannot explain. It could not account for the orderly motions of the planets, such as all orbiting the same way, or for planets that differ so much from the Sun (the Sun is nearly all hydrogen and helium, while the terrestrial planets are rock and metal). It also required a very rare near-collision between stars, which cannot explain the many planetary systems we see around most stars. Watching young stars form with disks in nebulae is different: it is direct support for the nebular theory rather than a failure of the close encounter idea itself.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a step in the stellar recycling process?
options: Stars release their chemical contents at the end of their lives, either gradually in the form of a planetary nebula, or more violently in a supernova explosion.
Radioactivity breaks down the large nuclei of heavy elements, ensuring there is sufficient hydrogen and helium for future generations of stars.
Nuclear fusion within stars produces elements with higher atomic numbers, up to iron in some stars.
Nebulae collapse under gravity, forming new stars.
quiz.why: Stellar recycling is: stars form in gas clouds, fusion builds heavier elements, dying stars return that material to space as a planetary nebula or supernova, and the enriched gas forms new stars. Radioactivity breaking down heavy nuclei is not a step, and hydrogen and helium were made in the Big Bang, not by decay. Fusion in stars building elements up to iron is a correct step.

quiz.q: Which of the following is most important in causing a cloud of gas to collapse to form a star and planets?
options: Pressure from other gas clouds pushes the gas inward.
Gravity pulls all the gas inward.
Pressure from light from nearby stars pushes the gas inward.
Opposite charges in the gas attract.
Some gas is sent outward, causing the rest to move inward to conserve momentum.
quiz.why: Gravity pulls every bit of gas toward all the rest, so when a cloud is dense enough gravity makes it collapse and form a star and planets. A shock wave from a nearby supernova may start the collapse, but it is gravity that keeps it going. Pressure from light or other clouds, attraction of opposite charges (the gas is neutral overall) and momentum from outward-flung gas are not the main cause.

quiz.q: If an interstellar gas cloud shrinks in size, what does the law of conservation of energy predict it will do?
options: spin slower
heat up
spin faster
cool off
continue shrinking
quiz.why: As the cloud shrinks, gravitational potential energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the falling gas. The particles collide and that motion becomes thermal energy, so the cloud heats up. Spinning faster is predicted by conservation of angular momentum, a different law. Cooling off or spinning slower is the opposite of what happens, and conservation of energy says nothing about it continuing to shrink.

quiz.q: If an interstellar gas cloud shrinks in size, what does the law of conservation of angular momentum predict it will do?
options: cool off
continue shrinking
spin faster
heat up
spin slower
quiz.why: A shrinking cloud has to spin faster to keep its angular momentum constant, just as a skater speeds up when she pulls in her arms. Heating up comes from conservation of energy, not angular momentum. Spinning slower would mean losing angular momentum, and cooling off or continuing to shrink are not predicted by this law.

quiz.q: According to our theory of solar system formation, why do all the planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same plane?
options: It is a coincidence, as we would expect that most other solar systems would not have all their planets orbiting in such a pattern.
Any planets that once orbited in the opposite direction or a different plane were ejected from the solar system.
The laws of conservation of energy and conservation of angular momentum ensure that any rotating, collapsing cloud will end up as a spinning disk.
The Sun formed first, and as it grew in size it spread into a disk, rather like the way a ball of dough can be flattened into a pizza by spinning it.
The original solar nebula happened to be disk shaped by chance.
quiz.why: A collapsing, rotating cloud heats up, spins faster and has its random motions smoothed out by collisions, so it flattens into a disk turning in one direction. The planets formed in that disk, so they orbit in the same direction and nearly the same plane. This is a natural result, not a coincidence or a clean-up of misfits. The Sun formed at the centre of the disk; it did not form first and then spread out like pizza dough.

quiz.q: Which of the following lists the ingredients of the solar nebula from highest to lowest percentage of mass of the nebula?
options: hydrogen compounds, hydrogen and helium gas, metals, rocks
hydrogen compounds, rocks, metals, hydrogen and helium gas
hydrogen compounds, hydrogen and helium gas, rocks, metals
hydrogen and helium gas, hydrogen compounds, metals, rocks
hydrogen and helium gas, hydrogen compounds, rocks, metals
quiz.why: By mass the solar nebula was about 98% hydrogen and helium gas, 1.4% hydrogen compounds (water, methane, ammonia), 0.4% rock and 0.2% metal. So the order from highest to lowest is hydrogen and helium gas, hydrogen compounds, rock, metal. The wrong lists put the gas lower or swap rock and metal with hydrogen compounds.

quiz.q: About what percentage of the mass of the solar nebula consisted of elements other than hydrogen and helium?
options: 2 percent
0 percent
0.1 percent
80 percent
20 percent
quiz.why: Hydrogen and helium made up about 98% of the nebula's mass, so everything else together (hydrogen compounds, rock and metal) was about 2%. Zero or 0.1% is too small to build the planets, and 20% or 80% would be far too much.

quiz.q: The very first generation of star systems in the universe must have been born from gas that consisted entirely of hydrogen and helium (and no other elements). Which of the following statements is most likely to have been true about these first-generation star systems?
options: They did not have any planets or asteroids or comets.
They had terrestrial planets but no jovian planets.
They did not have any disks of gas around them as they formed.
They had asteroids and comets but no large planets.
quiz.why: With only hydrogen and helium there is nothing that can condense into solid grains, so there would be no rock, metal or ice to build planetesimals. Without planetesimals there can be no asteroids or comets, and no planets either, because even gas giants grow from a solid core that then captures gas. Disks still form from any collapsing, spinning cloud, so the lack of a disk is not the answer.

quiz.q: What happened during the accretion phase of the early solar system?
options: Particles grew by colliding and sticking together.
Atoms of hydrogen and helium gas bonded together and solidified.
The solar nebula differentiated into metals inside of the frost line and ices beyond.
Earth gained its oceans from icy planetesimal capture.
Large planetesimals captured atmospheres from the solar nebula.
quiz.why: Accretion is the growth of solid particles: tiny grains stuck together, then planetesimals grew and pulled in others by gravity. Separating metals and rocks inside the frost line from ices beyond it was condensation, which came before. Earth's water arrived later through impacts, and hydrogen and helium gas do not bond and solidify in the nebula.

quiz.q: Which of the following accurately describes how the Jovian planetesimals were formed?
options: Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of rock and metal via static electricity and other non-gravitational forces. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting hydrogen compounds and hydrogen and helium gas from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula.
Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of hydrogen compounds via gravity. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting rocks and metals from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula.

Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of hydrogen compounds, rock, and metal via static electricity and other non-gravitational forces. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting hydrogen and helium gas from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula via gravity.

Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of hydrogen compounds, rock, and metal via gravity. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting hydrogen and helium gas from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula.
quiz.why: Beyond the frost line the tiny grains were a mix of ice (hydrogen compounds), rock and metal. Gravity is much too weak to pull such small specks together, so they stuck by static electricity and other non-gravitational forces. Only when planetesimals were large enough did their gravity start to attract hydrogen and helium gas. The wrong options either start the process with gravity on tiny grains or leave out part of the mix of ice, rock and metal.

quiz.q: How did most of the moons around Jovian planets come to be?
options: The Jovian moons are the scattered remnants of a fifth Jovian planet that was destroyed by an impact in the Heavy Bombardment, and which settled into orbit around the remaining Jovian planets.
Smaller planetesimals were gravitationally captured by the larger Jovian planetesimals and became the Jovian moons.
Parts of the Jovian planetesimals broke off in the accretion phase and became the Jovian moons.
They formed by accretion in much the same way that planets formed around the Sun in the protoplanetary nebula, but on a smaller scale.
quiz.why: The large moons of the jovian planets formed in disks of gas and dust around each growing giant planet, by accretion in the same way planets formed around the Sun but on a smaller scale. That is why they orbit in the planet's rotation direction in nearly circular orbits. They did not come from a destroyed fifth planet or break off the planets. A few small odd moons were captured, but capture needs an object to lose energy (for example to friction in the planet's gas), so simple gravitational capture is not how most moons formed.

quiz.q: The frost line of the solar system was located approximately between
options: the present-day orbits of Venus and Earth.
the present-day orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune.
the present-day orbits of Mercury and Venus.
the Sun and the present-day orbit of Mercury.
quiz.why: Hydrogen compounds freeze into ice only below about 150 K, and in the solar nebula that temperature was reached around 2.7 AU, which is between the present orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Between Mercury and Earth the nebula was too hot for ice, and the orbits of Uranus and Neptune are far beyond the frost line.

quiz.q: Why are the inner planets made of denser materials than the outer planets?
options: In the inner part of the nebula only metals and rocks were able to condense because of the high temperatures, whereas hydrogen compounds, although more abundant, were only able to condense in the cooler outer regions.

When the solar nebula formed a disk, materials naturally segregated into bands, and in our particular solar system, the denser materials settled nearer the Sun, while lighter materials are found in the outer part.
The Sun's gravity pulled denser materials toward the inner part of the solar nebula, while lighter gases escaped more easily.
In the beginning, when the protoplanetary disk was spinning faster, centrifugal forces flung the lighter materials toward the outer parts of the solar nebula.
Denser materials were heavier and sank to the center of the nebula.
quiz.why: Near the young Sun, ices such as water could not stay frozen, so the only solids available there were metal and rock, even though ice-forming material was more plentiful overall. Beyond the frost line ices could condense as well, so the outer planets gained lighter, icy material and far more of it. The Sun's gravity pulling dense material in, spinning flinging light material out, or dense material sinking are not what happened, because every ingredient orbits the Sun in the same way regardless of its density.

quiz.q: Hydrogen compounds in the solar nebula could condense into ice at temperatures of about 150 K. Suppose they instead could have condensed only at temperatures below 50 K? What would have been different in the solar nebula?
options: Jovian planets would have formed inside the frost line.
The frost line would have been farther from the Sun.
The frost line would have been closer to the Sun.
Terrestrial planets would have formed outside the frost line.
quiz.why: Ice can form only where the gas is colder than the temperature at which the compound condenses. If hydrogen compounds needed to be below 50 K instead of 150 K, the nebula would have to be much colder, which happens only farther from the Sun, so the frost line would be farther out. Terrestrial planets form inside the frost line and jovian planets outside it, so those other statements contradict the definition.

quiz.q: Observations of young stars suggest that when the Sun was young, the solar wind
options: was weaker than it is today.
was stronger than it is today.
was about the same strength as it is today.
was nonexistent.
blew outward only along the Sun's poles.
quiz.why: Young stars rotate fast and have strong magnetic fields, so they have much stronger winds and emit more high-energy radiation than older stars. The young Sun's strong wind and radiation helped blow away the leftover gas of the solar nebula. So it was stronger than today, not weaker, the same or absent, and the wind blew in all directions.

quiz.q: What might have happened if the hydrogen and helium gas pervading the early Solar System had not been driven out (i.e., if the solar nebula had not been cleared)?
options: The asteroids would have been able to assemble into a planet.
Accretion would have been stifled, leading to much smaller planets.
Only the Jovian planets would have grown much larger.
All planets would have grown much larger, and the terrestrial planets would have accreted hydrogen and helium gas.
quiz.why: If the hydrogen and helium had stayed, the nebula would have kept cooling until ices could form even in the inner Solar System, so the terrestrial planets could have grown larger and could have gathered hydrogen and helium gas, changing their basic nature. Asteroids do not assemble into a planet because the gas is cleared, and gas would not stifle growth or make only the jovian planets larger.

quiz.q: According to the nebular theory, what are asteroids and comets?
options: leftover planetesimals that never accreted into planets
chunks of rock or ice that condensed long after the planets had formed
the shattered remains of collisions between planets
the shattered remains of collisions between moons
chunks of rock or ice that have been expelled from the planets by volcanoes
quiz.why: Asteroids (rocky, from inside the frost line) and comets (icy, from beyond it) are leftover planetesimals that never became part of a planet. They did not form long after the planets, are not the remains of collisions between planets or moons, and are not volcanic debris.

quiz.q: What happened during the heavy bombardment?
options: Planetesimals collided with one another and stuck together to form planets.
A supernova disrupted a gas cloud, causing it to start collapsing to form the solar system.
The planets of the solar system suffered many impacts.
A large meteor collided with Earth, killing the dinosaurs.
The planets collided with one another.
quiz.why: Once the planets had formed, the leftover planetesimals kept slamming into them and their moons for a few hundred million years; this cratering era is the heavy bombardment. Planetesimals sticking together to form planets was accretion, which came earlier. A supernova may have triggered the nebula's collapse, the dinosaur impact happened about 66 million years ago, and the planets did not collide with each other.

quiz.q: What is the giant impact hypothesis for the origin of the Moon?
options: The Moon formed just like Earth, from accretion in the solar nebula.
The Moon formed from material blasted out of Earth's mantle and crust by the impact of a Mars-size object.
The Moon formed when two gigantic asteroids collided with one another.
The Moon originally was about the same size as Earth, but a giant impact blasted most of it away so that it ended up much smaller than Earth.
quiz.why: The giant impact hypothesis says a Mars-size object hit the young Earth, blasting material from Earth's outer rocky layers into orbit, where it gathered to form the Moon. The Moon did not form in the nebula like Earth, because its density and composition differ. It did not come from two asteroids colliding, and it was not once an Earth-sized body that lost most of its mass.

quiz.q: Which of the following does NOT directly support the giant impact hypothesis for the formation of our Moon?
options: The Moon is very quiet geologically compared to most other bodies.
The Moon lacks volatile chemicals that would vaporize in a large impact.
The Moon is very large for its host body, the Earth.
Computer simulations show that a collision between planetesimals can result in an Earth-Moon system like ours.
quiz.why: The Moon's lack of volcanism and tectonics is only a result of its small size, which let it cool quickly, and it says nothing about how the Moon formed. The other three do support the hypothesis: the missing volatile chemicals fit the heat of an impact vaporizing them, computer simulations can reproduce the Earth-Moon system, and the Moon's large size relative to Earth is what the impact idea explains and what capture cannot.

quiz.q: We know that Earth has water. However, according to our theory of solar system formation, the inner solar system was too hot for hydrogen compounds like water to condense. What do we conclude?
options: Earth's water likely was brought here by asteroids or comets that formed beyond the frost line.
Our theory of solar system formation will need modification because it is unable to account for the existence of water on Earth.
Water arrived on Earth at a time when it rained throughout the inner solar system.
Earth's water probably originated through chemical reactions among the rock and metal of Earth's interior.
quiz.why: The terrestrial planets formed where it was too hot for ice, so Earth's water was probably delivered by icy planetesimals, asteroids or comets that formed beyond the frost line and struck Earth during the heavy bombardment. The theory is therefore not broken by Earth's water. It did not rain throughout the inner nebula, and water does not come from chemical reactions of rock and metal alone.

quiz.q: According to our theory of solar system formation, why do we find some exceptions to the general rules and patterns of the planets?
options: The exceptions are probably the result of the Sun passing very close to another star billions of years ago.
The exceptions probably represent objects that formed recently, rather than early in the history of the solar system.
The exceptions probably represent objects that were captured by our solar system from interstellar space.
Most of the exceptions are the result of giant impacts or close gravitational encounters.
Our theory is not quite correct because it cannot explain these exceptions.
quiz.why: The nebular theory explains the general patterns with the collapse of the nebula, and it explains most exceptions, such as Uranus's tilt, Venus's backward spin and Earth's large Moon, by random events like giant impacts and close gravitational encounters among leftover planetesimals. A star passing close to the Sun is the discarded close encounter hypothesis. The exceptions are not recent objects, captured moons were mostly captured from material orbiting the Sun rather than interstellar space, and exceptions do not show the theory is wrong.

quiz.q: Suppose the Sun had been born with more mass, making it larger and hotter. Which of the following consequences would we expect according to the nebular theory?
options: Jovian planets would have formed farther from the Sun.
Asteroids would have formed closer to the Sun.
There would be no comets.
There would have been no solar nebula in which material could condense to form planets.
quiz.why: A more massive, hotter Sun would heat the nebula more, so the temperature low enough for ices to form would be reached farther from the Sun, and the frost line, where jovian planets form, would be farther out. Asteroids, which form inside the frost line, would also form farther out, not closer. Comets would still form, and a nebula would still exist.

quiz.q: Where can we find the BEST observational evidence of our current theory of Solar System formation?
options: In the spectra of stars.
In the dark matter halos of distant galaxies.
In nearby nebulae.
In the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud.
In supernova explosions of nearby stars.
quiz.why: In nearby clouds of gas we can watch stars forming right now, surrounded by flattened spinning disks of gas and dust, just as the nebular theory predicts for our own Sun.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of energy conversion processes that occurred in the formation of the early Solar System?
options: Heat energy was converted into gravitational potential energy as the solar nebula collapsed to form the Sun, and some of this potential energy was then converted into nuclear energy to kickstart the Sun's fusion reactions.
Gravitational potential energy was converted into kinetic energy as the nebula collapsed, and most of this energy was dissipated as heat and radiation.
Kinetic energy was converted into gravitational potential energy as the nebula collapsed, and this potential energy caused the Sun to shrink and spin faster.

Gravitational potential energy was converted to kinetic energy as the nebula collapsed, and most of this energy was converted into chemical energy to create the raw materials from which the planets could form.
Kinetic energy was converted into nuclear energy as the Sun formed, and some of this nuclear energy was converted into radiation to generate the solar wind.
quiz.why: As the cloud fell inward, gravitational potential energy became the motion (kinetic energy) of its particles. Collisions turned that motion into heat, and much of the heat escaped as radiation.

quiz.q: Why are the Jovian planets so much larger than the terrestrial planets?
options: The Jovian planetesimals formed earlier in the Solar System's history, allowing them to accrete more material than the terrestrial planets.
The Jovian planetesimals were cooler than the terrestrial ones, and could accrete hydrogen and helium gas onto them through condensation.
The Jovian planetesimals formed beyond the frost line for hydrogen and helium, which allowed them to capture these gases and grow larger than the terrestrial ones.

The Jovian planetesimals grew more quickly than the terrestrial ones since they could incorporate hydrogen compounds, and were thus able to capture large amounts of hydrogen and helium gas before it was cleared out by the solar wind.
The Jovian planetesimals simply had more material to assemble from, as their orbits were larger.
quiz.why: Beyond the frost line, ices of hydrogen compounds (water, methane, ammonia) could condense, so planetesimals there had far more solid material and grew big fast. Their strong gravity then pulled in hydrogen and helium gas before the young Sun's wind cleared it. The frost line is for hydrogen compounds, not hydrogen and helium, which never condense.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements best explains why all the major planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same plane?
options: The Sun's gravity is strongest at its equator, so it pulled all the planets into this orbital alignment.
The planets that did not orbit in the same direction and in different planes got destroyed by collisions or were flung out of the Solar System by gravity.
The Sun's rotation spun out the planets as it formed.
The planets originally orbited in different directions, but gravity later pulled them into an ordered formation.
The planets formed from a disk of rotating gas, and their orbits therefore match the direction and plane of the disk's rotation.
quiz.why: The collapsing nebula spun faster and flattened into a disk. Planets that grew within that spinning disk inherited its direction and its plane.

quiz.q: What is the correct timeline for the formation of the Solar System? (Hint: remember how long the heavy bombardment took, and what would have happened if the solar nebula had not been cleared fairly quickly.)
options: The solar nebula collapsed, the solar nebula was cleared, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the heavy bombardment ended.
The solar nebula collapsed, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the heavy bombardment ended, the solar nebula was cleared.
The solar nebula collapsed, the heavy bombardment ended, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the solar nebula was cleared.
The solar nebula collapsed, the solar nebula was cleared, the heavy bombardment ended, the planetesimals grew via accretion.
The solar nebula collapsed, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the solar nebula was cleared, the heavy bombardment ended.
quiz.why: Collapse came first, then planetesimals grew by accretion. The leftover gas was cleared early (otherwise the terrestrial planets would have kept gathering gas), and the heavy bombardment dragged on for a few hundred million years after that.

quiz.q: Which of the following did NOT happen during the heavy bombardment?
options: The Moon formed.
Earth acquired its water and life began to develop.
Planetesimals were flung by gravitational encounters in different directions, some becoming the moons of larger planetesimals.
The Sun formed at its current location and hydrogen fusion began.
Some planetesimals collided violently, resulting in unusual tilts or rotation directions.
quiz.why: The Sun formed and began fusion at the very start, when the centre of the collapsing nebula grew hot and dense, long before the bombardment by leftover planetesimals.

order.why: Metals condense below about 1000 to 1600 K, rock below about 500 to 1300 K and hydrogen compounds below about 150 K. Hydrogen and helium never condense in the nebula, so they belong at the top.

order.why: Right beside the Sun nothing could condense. Near Mercury's orbit metals and some rock formed grains; farther out, where Venus, Earth and Mars formed, more types of rock could. sort.title: What makes it happen?
sort.prompt: Sort each event in the collapsing solar nebula by its main cause.

items.text: The shrinking cloud heats up
Collapsing clouds glow in infrared light
Gravitational potential energy becomes thermal energy
The centre gets hot enough to form the Sun
The shrinking cloud spins faster
Much material stays in orbit instead of falling into the Sun
The young Sun spun very fast
A skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms
The lumpy cloud flattens into a disk
Elliptical orbits become nearly circular
Random up-and-down motions cancel out

sort.why: Energy conservation turns the energy of infalling gas into heat, making the hot centre and the infrared glow. Angular momentum conservation makes the shrinking cloud and the young Sun spin fast and keeps material orbiting in a disk. Collisions average out random motions, flattening the cloud and circularizing orbits.

sort.title: Terrestrial or jovian?
sort.prompt: Sort each fact by the kind of planet whose formation it describes.

items.text: Formed inside the frost line
Seeds made only of metal and rock
Built from less than 1% of the nebula's mass
Too small to capture hydrogen and helium gas
Leftovers became asteroids
Got water later from icy planetesimals
Formed beyond the frost line
Seeds of ice as well as metal and rock
Gravity pulled in huge amounts of hydrogen and helium
Surrounded by their own spinning disks
Large regular moons formed by accretion around them
Leftovers became comets

sort.why: Inside the frost line only metal and rock could condense, so the terrestrial planets were built from little material, stayed small and could not hold gas; their leftovers are rocky asteroids. Beyond it, ices added much more solid material, so large cores captured hydrogen and helium, had their own disks with moons, and left icy comets.

sort.title: Nebular theory or close encounter?
sort.prompt: Sort each statement by the idea it belongs to.

items.text: Planets form from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust
Proposed by Kant and Laplace
Predicts planetary systems should be common
Explains why planets orbit in one plane and one direction
Supported by disks seen around young stars
Planets are blobs of gas pulled out of the Sun
Needs another star to pass very close to the Sun
Makes planetary systems extremely rare
Cannot explain the two types of planets
Has been discarded

sort.why: The nebular theory treats planet formation as a normal part of star birth in a collapsing, spinning cloud, which explains the orderly motions and predicts many planetary systems. The close encounter hypothesis needed an extremely unlikely near-collision, could not explain the orbits or the two planet types, and has been discarded.

The Moon's rocks resemble Earth's mantle and crust
The Moon lacks water, sodium and zinc

sort.why: The simulations, the match with Earth's outer layers, the missing volatile substances, the lack of metal and the low density all point to the Moon being made from Earth's outer layers in a hot impact. Being geologically quiet and airless comes from the Moon's small size, being round from gravity, and keeping one face toward Earth from tides; these would be true however it formed.
